title: Lottery Tax by State: Exact Take-Home Amounts (2026)
description: Win $200M in Powerball? See exactly what you keep after federal and state taxes — state by state, down to the dollar.
content:
What This Article Actually Calculates and Why State Taxes Cost Winners Millions

If you won the Powerball jackpot tonight, here is exactly what you would take home in each state. Not a rough estimate. Not a ballpark. The specific dollar amount that hits your bank account after the federal government and your state both take their cut.

The base case for every calculation in this article: a $200 million Powerball jackpot, lump sum option, single filer. That is a realistic jackpot size — the November 4, 2026 Powerball draw just reset the jackpot cycle, and $200 million represents a mid-range prize that tens of millions of players are chasing. The math here applies proportionally to any jackpot size.

Why does lottery tax by state matter so much? Because where you live when you claim your ticket is worth more than most people realize. On a $200 million jackpot, the difference between the best and worst states for winners exceeds $10 million — money that evaporates purely based on your zip code, not your financial decisions. Use our lottery tax calculator to run your own numbers with any jackpot size and your specific state.

Federal Tax Calculation: How the IRS Takes 37% Before Your State Gets Involved

Federal taxes hit every winner the same way regardless of state. Here is how the math works on a $200 million jackpot.

Step 1: The Lump Sum Reduction

The advertised jackpot is paid in full only as a 30-year annuity. The lump sum cash value — what you actually receive immediately — is approximately 60% of the advertised amount. On a $200 million jackpot, the lump sum cash value is $120 million.

Note: The exact cash value percentage varies slightly by draw and current interest rates. The 60% figure is a standard approximation used for planning purposes.

Step 2: Federal Withholding at 24%

The lottery withholds 24% immediately on prizes over $5,000. On a $120 million lump sum, that is $28,800,000 withheld at the time of payout. You receive a check for approximately $91,200,000 after withholding.

Step 3: The Tax Return Reality — 37% Marginal Rate

The 24% withholding is not your final federal tax bill. When you file your return, the IRS taxes lottery winnings as ordinary income. For 2026, the top marginal federal rate is 37% for single filers on income above $626,350. A $120 million lump sum blows past that threshold entirely, so virtually all of your winnings are taxed at 37%.

Total federal tax on $120 million at 37%: $44,400,000. Subtract the $28,800,000 already withheld, and you owe an additional $15,600,000 when you file. Your total federal tax burden: $44,400,000. What remains after federal taxes only: $75,600,000.

This calculation simplifies the progressive bracket structure for clarity. In practice, the first $626,350 is taxed at lower bracket rates, adding a few thousand dollars back. For a jackpot this size, the difference is negligible and the effective rate is functionally 37%.

Lump Sum vs. Annuity Breakdown: Real Dollar Figures on a $200M Powerball Jackpot

Taking the Lump Sum

Lump sum gross: $120,000,000
Federal tax (37%): −$44,400,000
After federal taxes: $75,600,000
State tax varies (see table below)

Taking the Annuity

The annuity pays $200,000,000 over 30 years, with annual payments increasing by approximately 5% per year. The first annual payment on a $200 million jackpot is roughly $3,100,000, growing to over $12,000,000 by year 30. Each payment is taxed as ordinary income in the year received, still at the 37% federal rate for large payments, plus state income tax.

Total annuity payout after 37% federal tax over 30 years: approximately $126,000,000. This exceeds the lump sum net but requires waiting three decades and accepting the risk that tax laws change. Most financial advisors and winners choose the lump sum. This article focuses on lump sum figures because that is the choice the overwhelming majority of jackpot winners make.

The difference between winning in New York vs. Florida on a $200M Powerball jackpot is over $10 million — driven entirely by state income tax on lottery winnings.

State Rankings: Best and Worst States for Lottery Winners by Net Payout

Best States: Zero State Tax on Lottery Winnings

Nine states charge $0 in state income tax on lottery winnings, leaving winners with the full post-federal amount of $75,600,000 on a $200 million jackpot:

  • California — No state tax on lottery winnings (despite high income tax rates generally)
  • Florida — No state income tax at all
  • Texas — No state income tax at all
  • Washington — No state income tax at all
  • Wyoming — No state income tax at all
  • South Dakota — No state income tax at all
  • Tennessee — No state income tax at all
  • New Hampshire — No state income tax on earned income or lottery winnings
  • Pennsylvania — Specifically exempts lottery winnings from state income tax

Worst States: Highest State Tax Burden on Winners

  1. New York — 10.9% — Take-home: $62,520,000 (or as low as $57,870,000 for NYC residents)
  2. New Jersey — 10.75% — Take-home: $62,700,000
  3. Oregon — 9.9% — Take-home: $63,720,000
  4. Minnesota — 9.85% — Take-home: $63,780,000
  5. Maryland — 8.95% — Take-home: $64,860,000

The gap between winning in a no-tax state versus winning in New York: $13,080,000. That is not a rounding error. That is the price of residency — and it is entirely avoidable if a winner legally establishes residency in a no-tax state before claiming their prize. Consult a tax attorney before making any residency change for tax purposes — the rules around domicile are complex and state tax authorities scrutinize large prize claims carefully.
